analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent, permanently repeals the estate tax, and permanently eases the AMT.
analysis.headline: S. 336 drew no cosponsors and died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the expiration dates (called sunsets) on the 2001 and 2003 tax cut laws, so their lower income-tax rates and the reduced rates on capital gains and dividends would never run out. It would also permanently repeal the federal estate tax on large inheritances, and permanently raise the exemption for the alternative minimum tax so fewer households owe it. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received any further action, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest gains go to high-income households, whose top tax rates, capital gains rates, and dividend rates would be locked in permanently, and to the heirs of very large estates, who would owe no estate tax. Middle-income taxpayers would benefit too, mostly through the AMT exemption increase, which protects them from a parallel tax originally aimed at the very rich.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large-estate heirs

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sunset provisions of the 2001 and 2003 tax cut laws so their rate reductions become permanent rather than expiring at the end of 2012 [S2][S3].
Permanently repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for deaths and gifts after December 31, 2009, eliminating tax on large inheritances [S2][S3].

Sets a schedule of rising alternative minimum tax exemptions through 2021 (for example $74,450 for joint filers in 2011) and lets most nonrefundable credits offset the AMT, shielding middle- and upper-middle-income households from a tax meant for the very rich [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Whatever services or programs federal revenues fund would bear the cost of permanently lower rates, and the burden falls hardest at the top: the bill's main dollar benefits go to the highest earners and the largest estates. A separate provision would repeal the refundable adoption credit added by the Affordable Care Act, reducing help for some adoptive families [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill's central provisions — permanent low rates and permanent estate-tax repeal — concentrate their dollar value on the top of the income scale, since high earners pay most income tax at top rates and only very large estates owe the estate tax [S2][S3].

It repeals the refundable adoption tax credit created by the Affordable Care Act, taking away refundable help (aid paid even to families with little tax owed) that the bill's AMT fixes do not restore [S3].

Permanently locking in all of the 2001 and 2003 cuts removes the deadline that had forced Congress to weigh the cost of those tax cuts against other priorities, an honest supporter would acknowledge that the changes were originally given expiration dates precisely to keep their long-term budget cost under review.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The AMT fix is a genuine benefit for middle-income families, because without it the alternative minimum tax — a second tax computation originally aimed at the very rich — would sweep in millions of ordinary households. But that fix is bundled with the bill's main purpose: making low top rates and capital-gains rates permanent and eliminating the estate tax entirely, changes whose dollar value is concentrated among the wealthiest households. The bill offers no offsetting revenue, so the whole cost lands on future federal budgets. A narrower AMT-only bill would have delivered the broadly shared benefit without the top-heavy permanence.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which took no action on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim DeMint introduced the bill on February 14, 2011 [S1][S5].

After being read twice, it was referred to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction; that referral is the last action in the bill's history, and no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote followed before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The 2010 law had extended the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts only temporarily, which meant the question of who pays for them would have to be revisited; because the bill died, the high-income rate cuts and full estate-tax repeal it sought were never locked in during that Congress, and the debate stayed open for the next round of negotiations.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Anyone wanting the tax-cut question reopened

for.name: Sen. Jim DeMint
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 14, 2011, proposing permanent extension of the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts, permanent estate-tax repeal, and permanent AMT relief.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Sen. Max Baucus, D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 14, 2011 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, and the bill's only recorded support was its Republican sponsor; it drew zero cosponsors from either party [S4].

industries.note: Permanent extension of the 2001/2003 rate cuts locks in lower top rates and the reduced capital-gains and dividend rates, whose largest dollar value goes to the highest earners. The cost of those rates shows up as forgone federal revenue rather than a bill any household pays directly.
Permanent estate-tax repeal means inheritances of any size would never be taxed; the benefit is exclusive to the very largest estates, since smaller estates were already exempt.
The AMT exemption schedule keeps families with children and high local-tax deductions out of a tax meant for the very rich, a broadly shared benefit bundled into the bill.
